title: Design an Undo/Redo Text Editor
statement_md:
*Gang of Four pattern: **Command** (behavioral). An edit is reified as an
object, not just a mutation — so it can be undone later by something that
never had to understand how it was made.*

Design a plain-text `Editor` that supports multi-level undo/redo. Implement:

- `Editor()` starts with an empty document (`""`) and empty undo/redo history.
- `append(text)` adds `text` to the end of the document and returns the
  document. It's a new command: it clears any pending redo history.
- `delete(k)` removes the last `k` characters and returns the document. If `k`
  exceeds the document's length, it clears the whole document instead of
  erroring. This also clears the redo history. `delete(0)` is a legal no-op
  command — it still counts as one entry in the undo history.
- `undo()` reverts the most recent command (whether it was `append` or
  `delete`) and returns the resulting document. If there's nothing to undo,
  the document is unchanged. The reverted command moves onto the redo history.
- `redo()` re-applies the most recently undone command and returns the
  resulting document. If there's nothing to redo, the document is unchanged.
  The re-applied command moves back onto the undo history.
- `history()` returns the names of the commands currently on the undo stack,
  oldest first — `"append"` or `"delete"` — reflecting only what's actually
  undoable right now (an undone command leaves this list until it's redone).

Every operation should store and rewind only `O(k)` state of its own, where
`k` is the length of the text being appended or deleted — never a copy of the
whole document per command, and never work proportional to the number of past
commands. Every call returns the current document, so the return itself is
unavoidably proportional to the document's length; that is not the cost this
problem is about.
constraints: At most $10^4$ calls total across `append`, `delete`, `undo`, `redo`, and `history`.
The document's length never exceeds $2 \times 10^4$ characters.

solutions.title: Snapshot the Document on Every Command
solutions.intuition_md:
The most direct way to make an edit reversible is to remember what the
document looked like *before* it, and restore that snapshot on undo. Each
undo-stack entry is just `(command name, prior document)`; `undo` pops one and
swaps the current document back to the saved string, pushing the same pair
(now paired with the document being left) onto the redo stack.

This is easy to get right and easy to verify — there's no logic split across
two directions to keep in sync, because "undo" and "redo" are the same
operation (pop, swap, push onto the other stack) run against opposite stacks.
The cost is memory and, for `append`, time: each entry stores an entire copy of
the document, so `k` edits into an `n`-character document cost `O(n)` per
undo-stack push, not `O(\text{edit length})` — the snapshot is the whole
string regardless of how small the edit was.
solutions.algorithm_md:
Keep `doc` plus two stacks of `(name, snapshot)` pairs. `append`/`delete` both
push `(name, doc)` — the state *before* the edit — onto `undo_stack`, clear
`redo_stack`, then compute the new `doc`.

- `undo`: pop `(name, before)` from `undo_stack`, push `(name, doc)` (the
  state being left) onto `redo_stack`, set `doc = before`.
- `redo`: pop `(name, after)` from `redo_stack`, push `(name, doc)` onto
  `undo_stack`, set `doc = after`.
- `history`: the `name` half of every `undo_stack` entry, in stack order
  (oldest first, since entries are only ever appended at the end).
solutions.code:
class Editor:
    def __init__(self):
        self.doc = ""
        self.undo_stack = []  # (name, snapshot-before) pairs
        self.redo_stack = []

    def append(self, text: str) -> str:
        self.undo_stack.append(("append", self.doc))
        self.redo_stack.clear()
        self.doc += text
        return self.doc

    def delete(self, k: int) -> str:
        self.undo_stack.append(("delete", self.doc))
        self.redo_stack.clear()
        self.doc = self.doc[: max(0, len(self.doc) - k)]
        return self.doc

    def undo(self) -> str:
        if not self.undo_stack:
            return self.doc
        name, before = self.undo_stack.pop()
        self.redo_stack.append((name, self.doc))
        self.doc = before
        return self.doc

    def redo(self) -> str:
        if not self.redo_stack:
            return self.doc
        name, after = self.redo_stack.pop()
        self.undo_stack.append((name, self.doc))
        self.doc = after
        return self.doc

    def history(self) -> list[str]:
        return [name for name, _ in self.undo_stack]
solutions.time_complexity: O(n)\text{ per command, where } n \text{ is the document length}
solutions.time_complexity_reason: Pushing a command copies the entire current document string onto the stack, regardless of how much text the edit itself touches.
solutions.space_complexity_reason: Every one of the h entries across both stacks holds a full copy of the document at that point in history.

solutions.title: Command Pattern (Reified, Self-Reversing Edits)
solutions.intuition_md:
The Gang of Four's Command pattern reifies each edit as its own object with
two methods, `execute` and `undo`, instead of storing a snapshot of the whole
document. `Append` needs no state to undo itself — it just trims off the
`len(text)` characters it added. `Delete` does need state, but only the
characters it actually removed, captured once at `execute` time — the command
carries exactly the information its own reversal needs, nothing more.

This is the payoff: what each command *stores* is proportional to its own edit
rather than to the document, so the history stops carrying a full copy per
entry. Rebuilding the returned text is still `O(n)` — Python strings are
immutable and every operation hands back the whole document — so the win is
in memory, not in the per-call rebuild. It also generalizes
cleanly — a new command type (`Replace`, say) plugs in by implementing the same
two methods, with no change to `Editor.undo`/`redo`, which only ever call
through the `Command` interface and never inspect which concrete type they
have. The trade-off: for an editor whose commands are all cheap to snapshot
anyway (as here — plain-text `append`/`delete` never had an expensive
snapshot), that generality doesn't buy correctness, only a cleaner asymptotic
bound and a cleaner extension point.
solutions.algorithm_md:
A `Command` base class declares `execute(doc) -> doc` and `undo(doc) -> doc`;
`Editor` never subclasses on its own, it only ever calls through this
interface.

- `Append.execute` concatenates; `Append.undo` slices off the same length it
  added — no separate state needed, the command's own `text` is enough.
- `Delete.execute` slices off the last `k` characters (clamped to the
  document's length) and **saves what it removed** in `self.removed`, since
  undoing a delete means putting back characters `Delete` itself doesn't get
  handed again; `Delete.undo` appends `self.removed` back.
- `Editor._run(command)` is the one place that touches both stacks: apply the
  command, push it onto `undo_stack`, clear `redo_stack`.
- `undo`/`redo` pop a `Command` from one stack, call its `undo`/`execute`, and
  push it onto the other — the two directions differ only in which method they
  call and which stack they push to.
- `history` reads `command.name` off `undo_stack`, same shape as solution 0.
solutions.time_complexity: O(n + k)\text{ per operation, of which } O(k) \text{ is the edit}
solutions.time_complexity_reason: Each command stores and rewinds only the k characters its own edit concerns. Producing the returned document still rebuilds n characters, because Python strings are immutable and every operation returns the whole text — what the pattern removes is the per-command copy, not that rebuild.
solutions.space_complexity_reason: Each of the h stacked commands stores only its own edit (text.length for Append, the removed fragment for Delete), not a document-sized snapshot.
